title: A commercial exploration agreement is announced
summary: Apptronik announced an agreement with Mercedes-Benz to identify Apollo applications in manufacturing and described intended logistics and inspection use cases. It did not publish a site-specific operating result, robot count or reliability measurement.
basis: Reconstructed solely from Apptronik's dated March 2024 commercial-agreement announcement.
facts: Apptronik described its first publicly announced commercial Apollo deployment agreement. | Potential use cases included delivering kitted parts and inspecting components. | The announcement discussed intended manufacturing applications rather than measured operation.
limitations: The source did not establish a named factory operating result. | Commercial agreement language did not fill any tracked reliability field.

title: Mercedes documents production-environment training
summary: Mercedes-Benz confirmed Apollo robots at its Berlin Digital Factory Campus, production-environment data collection and employee teaching through teleoperation and augmented reality. The source established the operating-mode boundary but still published no runtime or reliability result.
basis: Reconstructed cumulatively from Apptronik's 2024 agreement and Mercedes-Benz's dated 18 March 2025 campus report.
facts: Mercedes-Benz confirmed multiple Apollo robots at the Berlin-Marienfelde campus. | Employees transferred production knowledge through teleoperation and augmented reality. | Mercedes said the robots were learning to act autonomously.
limitations: Training interaction is disclosed, but operational intervention frequency is not. | No operating hours, task output, downtime, failure or recovery result was published.
fleet_size_label: Multiple robots described; exact count unknown

title: GXO confirms a proof-of-concept pilot
summary: GXO publicly confirmed a Digit pilot for moving totes between autonomous mobile robots and a conveyor. The operator described the workflow but did not publish operating hours, output, failures, downtime, interventions or fleet size.
basis: Reconstructed from GXO's dated proof-of-concept announcement using only information public in that source.
facts: GXO identified the facility and the AMR-to-conveyor tote workflow. | The deployment stage was a proof-of-concept pilot.
limitations: No tracked reliability field had a qualifying public value. | A described workflow did not establish commercial operation or measured reliability.

title: The pilot becomes a commercial agreement
summary: GXO and Agility announced a multi-year Robots-as-a-Service agreement and described Digit robots as fully operational in the live warehouse. Commercial maturity advanced, but the announcement added no quantified runtime, output, availability, failures or intervention data.
basis: Reconstructed cumulatively from GXO's pilot announcement and the dated June 2024 commercial deployment announcements.
facts: Agility identified 5 June 2024 as the start of commercial operations. | GXO and Agility announced a multi-year RaaS agreement on 27 June 2024. | The announcement described multiple Digit robots but did not state the deployed count.
limitations: Commercial status is not a reliability metric. | No denominator allowed availability, task success or intervention rate to be calculated.

title: A multi-week factory trial becomes public
summary: BMW confirmed that Figure 02 had inserted sheet-metal parts during a trial lasting several weeks. It published no operating hours, output count, downtime, failure count or intervention count, and said no Figure robots remained at the plant after the trial.
basis: Reconstructed from BMW Group's dated trial release using only information public in that source.
facts: BMW described a trial lasting several weeks in a real body-shop process. | Figure 02 inserted sheet-metal parts into fixtures for chassis assembly. | BMW stated that no Figure robots remained at the plant and gave no timetable for a return.
limitations: The autonomy wording was attributable to Figure, not a quantified BMW measurement. | No denominator allowed a reliability or success rate to be calculated.

title: Quantified runtime and output appear
summary: Figure reported 1,250+ operating hours, 90,000+ parts and an 11-month deployment. The manufacturer also said every intervention was logged and described minimal hardware failures, but published neither count nor rate.
basis: Reconstructed from the 2024 BMW trial release and Figure's dated final Figure 02 deployment report.
facts: Figure reported 1,250+ operating hours and 90,000+ parts loaded. | Figure described 10-hour shifts from Monday through Friday. | Figure disclosed that interventions were logged and identified the forearm as the top hardware failure point.
limitations: The new totals were manufacturer-reported at this point in the source chronology. | Scheduled time, downtime, fleet size, intervention count, MTBF and MTTR remained unpublished.

title: BMW corroborates the headline totals
summary: BMW subsequently confirmed approximately 1,250 operating hours, more than 90,000 components and ten months of production support. The numbers moved from manufacturer-only reporting to operator corroboration, while core reliability denominators remained absent.
basis: Reconstructed cumulatively from the 2024 BMW release, Figure's 2025 report and BMW Group's dated 2026 production release.
facts: BMW confirmed around 1,250 operating hours and more than 90,000 moved components. | BMW tied the result to ten months and ten-hour weekday shifts. | Operator corroboration strengthened the provenance of the runtime and output totals.
limitations: The source still did not publish scheduled robot time, downtime, fleet size or intervention frequency. | The ten-month BMW scope and Figure's earlier 11-month deployment description were not reconciled.

summary: BMW subsequently confirmed approximately 1,250 operating hours, more than 90,000 components and ten months of production support. Runtime and output moved from manufacturer-only reporting to operator corroboration; the autonomy description remained attributable to Figure and core reliability denominators remained absent.
basis: Correction to HU-R001-H003 after separating the BMW-hosted operator account from autonomy wording attributable to Figure. The runtime and output corroboration is unchanged.

title: Humanoid publishes quantified POC results
summary: Humanoid reported a two-week Siemens factory POC, 60 tote moves per hour, above-90% autonomous pick-and-place success, more than 30 minutes of continuous autonomous execution and uptime exceeding eight hours. At this stage, the quantified results were manufacturer-reported.
basis: Reconstructed solely from Humanoid's dated 15 January 2026 account; Siemens had not yet published its own results statement.
facts: Humanoid described a two-week on-site POC at Siemens' Erlangen electronics factory. | The manufacturer reported 60 tote moves per hour and above-90% autonomous pick-and-place success. | The manufacturer separately reported more than 30 minutes of continuous autonomous execution and uptime exceeding eight hours.
limitations: The source did not define the uptime denominator or observation continuity. | Attempts, intervention frequency, downtime, MTBF and MTTR were not published.

title: Siemens corroborates the factory results
summary: Siemens confirmed the autonomous tote workflow, 60 moves per hour, uptime exceeding eight hours and above-90% autonomous pick-and-place success. Four tracked fields moved from manufacturer-only reporting to operator corroboration; the missing reliability denominators did not change.
basis: Reconstructed cumulatively from Humanoid's January report and Siemens' dated 16 April 2026 press release.
facts: Siemens confirmed the robot and autonomous tote-handling workflow at its Erlangen factory. | Siemens repeated the throughput, uptime and autonomous success figures. | The provenance strengthened even though the numeric values did not change.
limitations: Operator corroboration does not supply the missing uptime definition or observation window. | No intervention, downtime, failure or recovery counts were published.

title: Independent safety measurements become public
summary: Fraunhofer IPA published collision-force measurements for one Unitree G1 test unit and described the test repetitions and measurement setup. Energy endurance, field runtime, availability and failure-recovery metrics were not part of this public state.
basis: Reconstructed solely from Fraunhofer IPA's dated October 2025 safety guide.
facts: Fraunhofer identified one Unitree G1 test robot with Dex3-1 hands. | The guide reported average peak forces from at least three trials per collision scenario. | Forward walking collisions were reported at approximately 510 N at the chest and 530 N at the abdomen.
limitations: The guide labels the configuration G1 EDU+; the later benchmark publication specifies EDU-4 and firmware 1.04. | Safety-test results are not deployment uptime or field reliability measurements.

title: The broader independent benchmark is announced
summary: Fraunhofer specified the tested EDU-4 configuration and added independently derived per-charge endurance, cleanroom, stability and cybersecurity findings. The typical energy scenario reached 1:49 hours, but this was not a continuous field run or measured availability.
basis: Reconstructed cumulatively from the dated safety material and Fraunhofer IPA's 27 May 2026 benchmark press release.
facts: Fraunhofer specified G1 EDU-4, Dex3-1 hands and firmware 1.04. | Fraunhofer reported 1:49 hours for a typical standing-and-walking scenario and 2:49 hours while standing. | The release added independently assessed collision, stability, cleanroom and cybersecurity findings.
limitations: The endurance figures were scenario-derived single-charge results, not cumulative operating hours. | No scheduled time, downtime, MTBF, MTTR or intervention rate was published.

title: Detailed measurements expose the operating boundary
summary: Fraunhofer's detailed publication added mean power, walking speed, thermal, stability and recovery context and clarified that remote-controlled walking was the delivered baseline. The evidence became deeper without becoming a field-uptime record.
basis: Reconstructed cumulatively from all dated Fraunhofer sources available through 3 June 2026.
facts: Mean power in the defined typical scenario was 239 W. | Slow and fast walking were measured at 0.49 m/s and 0.84 m/s using 3D tracking. | The delivered baseline supported remote-controlled walking; further capabilities required user implementation.
limitations: Laboratory measurements should not be generalized into field availability or fleet reliability. | The results apply to the identified hardware and software state.
